## In this session you will learn to

1.  Create objects, use vectors, and call functions
2.  Install packages (once) and load them (every session)

# Part 1: R basics

Before we open any data, a few building blocks you'll use in every line of R. Type these in your script and run each line with **Cmd + Return** (Mac) or **Ctrl + Enter** (Windows); the result appears in the **Console**.

## Objects and the assignment arrow `<-`

`<-` stores a value in an **object** so you can use it later. Read it as "gets". The object appears in the **Variables** pane.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 1.1** — Store a number in an object called `my_age`, then add 5 to it.

Pattern: `OBJECT_NAME <- VALUE`
:::

```{r}
my_age <- 35
my_age
my_age + 5
```

## Vectors

`c()` combines values into a **vector**. Every value in a vector has the same type.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 1.2** — Make a vector of ages with `c()`, then find the `mean()`.
:::

```{r}
ages <- c(2, 18, 56, 61)
mean(ages)
```

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 1.3** — Make a vector of hospital names (text needs quotes!) and find its `length()`.
:::

```{r}
hospitals <- c("Central Hospital", "Military Hospital", "Other")
length(hospitals)
```

## Functions and arguments

A **function** does something to its inputs (**arguments**): `function_name(argument1, argument2, ...)`. Arguments can be named.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 1.4** — Use `round(3.14159)` with and without `digits = 2`.
:::

```{r}
round(3.14159)
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```

::: callout-tip
## Getting help

Type `?round` in the Console to open the help page for any function.
:::

## Data frames

A **data frame** is a table: each **column** is a variable (a vector), each **row** is an observation. (Later you'll also see **tibbles**: the tidyverse version of a data frame, which prints more neatly.)

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 1.5** — Make a small data frame with `data.frame()`, then pull out one column with `$`.

Pattern: `data.frame(COLUMN_1 = c(...), COLUMN_2 = c(...))`
:::

```{r}
patients <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cho"),
  age  = c(34, 51, 27)
)
patients

patients$age        # $ pulls out one column
```

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   R is **case-sensitive**: `Age` and `age` are different
-   Text needs quotes (`"Central Hospital"`); object names do not (`my_age`)
-   Every `(` needs a `)` — Positron highlights the matching pair
-   `#` starts a comment; R ignores the rest of the line
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 1 (2 min): objects and functions

Store three temperatures, 38.5, 39.1, and 37.9, in an object called `my_temps`. Then find their `mean()`.

✅ **Check:** the mean is 38.5

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
my_temps <- c(38.5, 39.1, 37.9)
mean(my_temps)
```

:::

# Part 2: Installing and loading packages

A **package** is a collection of functions someone else wrote. There are two steps:

| Step    | Function             | How often                 | Analogy                 |
|---------|----------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------|
| Install | `install.packages()` | **Once** per computer     | Buying a book           |
| Load    | `library()`          | **Every** time you open R | Taking it off the shelf |

Install everything for the whole workshop series (skip this if you did the [Setup](../setup.qmd)):

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "rio", "janitor", "skimr", "gtsummary", "flextable", "scales"))
```

Load only what you need today:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 2.1** — Load today's packages, one `library()` line each. ✅ You should see no line that starts with "Error".

Pattern: `library(PACKAGE_NAME)`
:::

```{r}
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling (dplyr) and plotting (ggplot2)
library(here)        # file paths that work on any computer
library(rio)         # import() and export() for almost any file type
library(skimr)       # skim() for a quick data summary
library(janitor)     # get_dupes() today; clean_names() in Session 2
```

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Package names need quotes in `install.packages()` but **not** in `library()`.
-   Red text is not always an error! Messages like "Attaching core tidyverse packages" are normal. An error starts with **Error**.
:::

# Part 3: Project folders and `here()`

## Why keep everything in one project folder?

-   **Organization:** data, scripts, and outputs live in one folder with a predictable structure (`raw_data/`, `processed_data/`, `student_scripts/`)
-   **Reproducibility:** the project works on any computer — yours, a collaborator's, future you's
-   **Shareable:** zip the folder and send it, or put it on GitHub

## Open the project folder for this class

1.  Download the workshop folder and save it somewhere you can find it (not your Downloads folder)
2.  In Positron, choose **File → Open Folder...**, select the `cwml-r-workshop` folder, and click **Open**. Positron uses that folder as the working directory
3.  Check the **Explorer** on the left: it should list the workshop files (`raw_data`, `student_scripts`, ...)

::: callout-tip
## Your own projects later

Make a new folder for each project (with subfolders like `raw_data/` and `scripts/`), and open it in Positron with **File → Open Folder...**. Add an empty file called `.here` at the top so `here()` always finds it.
:::

## Relative vs absolute paths

-   **Bad (absolute):** `"/Users/mwegener/Desktop/maybe_here/data.csv"` — only works on one computer
-   **Good (relative):** `here("raw_data", "data.csv")` — works on any computer that has the project folder

`here()` finds the top of the project folder (it looks for a `.here` file, which the workshop folder has) and builds the path from there.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.1** — Find the top of the project folder.

Pattern: `here::here()`
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
here::here()                                   # where is the top of my project?
```

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.2** — Build the path to `raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx`.

Pattern: `here::here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.EXTENSION")`
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
here::here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx")    # full path to a file inside it
```

`here::here()` means "the `here()` function from the here package". The `::` lets you use a function before loading its package.

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 2 (1 min): a path to the practice data

Build the path to the practice data, `raw_data/measles_raw.csv`.

✅ **Check:** the output ends in `.../raw_data/measles_raw.csv`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
#| eval: false
here::here("raw_data", "measles_raw.csv")
```
:::
:::

# Part 4: Importing data

## `import()` + `here()`

`rio::import()` reads almost any file type (`.csv`, `.xlsx`, `.txt`, SPSS, Stata, SAS, ...). It works out the type from the file extension, so you only need to learn one function. Save the result with `<-`, or it only prints to the Console and is gone.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 4.1** — Import `raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx` and call it `linelist_raw`.

Pattern: `NEW_NAME <- import(here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.EXTENSION"))`
:::

```{r}
linelist_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx"))
```

The same function works for other file types:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 4.2** — Import `raw_data/case_info.csv` (`case_info`) and `raw_data/hosp_info.txt` (`hosp_info`).
:::

```{r}
case_info <- import(here("raw_data", "case_info.csv"))   # comma-separated
hosp_info <- import(here("raw_data", "hosp_info.txt"))   # tab-separated text
```

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   File names must match exactly, including capitals and the extension.
-   "Error: No such file" means the folder or file name is misspelled, or the workshop folder isn't open (check the **Explorer** on the left).
:::

::: callout-tip
## Other import options you may see

-   **Base R:** `read.csv()` — older, slower, and needs more settings
-   **readr:** `read_csv()` — the tidyverse version, fast and returns a tibble
-   **haven:** `read_sav()`, `read_dta()`, `read_sas()` — SPSS, Stata, SAS files
-   **Excel files with several sheets:** `import(here("raw_data", "file.xlsx"), which = "Sheet2")`
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 3 (2 min): import the practice data

✅ **Check:** in the **Variables** pane, `measles_raw` shows 1215 rows and 11 columns

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "measles_raw.csv"))
```

# Part 5: Inspecting data

**Always look before you clean.** Inspecting tells you whether the data imported correctly and what needs fixing.

## Size and structure

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.1** — Size and structure of `linelist_raw`: `view()`, `dim()`, `names()`, `head()`, and `glimpse()` (the next three code blocks).
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
view(linelist_raw)       # opens the Data Explorer (or click the table icon next to it in the Variables pane)
```

```{r}
dim(linelist_raw)        # rows, columns
names(linelist_raw)      # column names
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: what is wrong with these column names?

Spaces, dots, capitals, and a mix of styles (`Case ID`, `date.onset`, `OUTCOME`). They are hard to type and need special handling. We fix all of them in Session 2 with one function.
:::

```{r}
head(linelist_raw)       # first 6 rows
glimpse(linelist_raw)    # every column, its type, and the first few values
```

In `glimpse()`, the type is shown in angle brackets: `<chr>` text, `<dbl>` number, `<date>` date, `<dttm>` date-time.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: which column types look wrong?

-   `date.onset` is `<chr>` (text) but the other dates are `<dttm>` (date-time)
-   `age` is `<chr>` — it should be a number
-   There is an `age_unit` column — are all ages in years?
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 4 (3 min): size and structure

Use `dim()` and `glimpse()` on `measles_raw`.

a)  Which column should be a number but is stored as text (`<chr>`)?
b)  Which column names will need backticks?

✅ **Check:** `dim()` gives 1215 11

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
dim(measles_raw)
glimpse(measles_raw)
```

a)  `Age (years)` is `<chr>` — it contains "unknown" and the code "999"
b)  Names with spaces or symbols need backticks: `` `Patient ID` ``, `` `Report Date` ``, `` `Age (years)` ``, `` `Vaccinated?` ``, `` `Temp (C)` ``, `` `Days in Hospital` ``
:::
:::

## Summary of every column

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.2** — `skim(linelist_raw)`. Look at `n_missing`, and the min and max of `wt_kg` and `ht_cm`.
:::

```{r}
skim(linelist_raw)
```

Look at the `n_missing` column, the minimum of `wt_kg` (below zero!), and the maximum of `ht_cm` (almost 3 meters!).

## Categories: `count()`

`count()` shows every distinct value in a column and how often it appears. It's the fastest way to find misspellings.

The data goes first, then the column: `count(DATA, COLUMN)`.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.3** — `count()` the hospital, Gender, OUTCOME, and age_unit columns.

Pattern: `count(DATA, COLUMN)`
:::

```{r}
count(linelist_raw, hospital)
count(linelist_raw, Gender)
count(linelist_raw, OUTCOME)
count(linelist_raw, age_unit)
```

::: callout-note
## 🔁 The base R way: `table()`

You will often see base R's `table()` in other people's code. It counts too, but **it hides missing values** unless you ask for them:

::: follow-along
**🔁 Follow along 5.4** — The base R way: `table()` OUTCOME, with and without `useNA = "ifany"`.
:::

```{r}
table(linelist_raw$OUTCOME)                   # where are the missing outcomes?
table(linelist_raw$OUTCOME, useNA = "ifany")  # there they are: 1493
```

`count()` always shows `NA`. With `table()`, add `useNA = "ifany"`. See [Base R ↔ tidyverse](../base-vs-tidyverse.qmd) for more translations.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 5 (3 min): categories

a)  `count()` District, SEX, and `` `Vaccinated?` `` in `measles_raw`. How many different ways is "North" written? How many ways is "No" written?
b)  Now try `table(measles_raw$District)`. What is missing compared with `count()`?

✅ **Check:** a) `count(District)` shows 18 rows (including NA) b) `table()` has no `NA`: 34 cases disappear

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
count(measles_raw, District)
count(measles_raw, SEX)
count(measles_raw, `Vaccinated?`)

table(measles_raw$District)                   # b) no NA!
table(measles_raw$District, useNA = "ifany")
```

"North" is written 4 ways ("North", "north", "Nroth", "North District"), and so is "No" ("No", "no", "N", "NO"). `table()` silently drops the 34 cases with no district; `useNA = "ifany"` brings them back. It also sorts lower-case values first, so "central" and "Central" are listed apart.
:::
:::

## Zooming in: `filter()` and `arrange()`

-   `filter()` keeps **rows** that meet a condition
-   `arrange()` sorts rows (`desc()` for largest first)

Each one takes the data first. Column names with spaces need **backticks**: `` `Case ID` ``. (The backtick key is at the top left of most keyboards.) Another reason to clean the names!

`linelist_raw` is a regular data frame, so R prints **every** row it gets — all 6,604 of them, with 12 columns each! To do **two** things, such as filtering and then showing only the first 10 rows, put one function **inside** another. R runs the inside first:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.5** — Use `filter()`, `arrange()`, and `head()` to find the patients with ages in months, the smallest weights, and the tallest patients (the next two code blocks).
:::

```{r}
# How many patients have ages in months?
nrow(filter(linelist_raw, age_unit == "months"))

# Show the first 10 of them
head(filter(linelist_raw, age_unit == "months"), 10)
```

```{r}
# Impossible weights: sort smallest first, then show the first 10 rows
head(arrange(linelist_raw, wt_kg), 10)

# Tallest patients: desc() sorts largest first
head(arrange(linelist_raw, desc(ht_cm)), 10)
```

::: callout-note
## Reading code from the inside out

`head(arrange(linelist_raw, wt_kg), 10)` reads: take `linelist_raw`, **arrange** it by weight, then take the **head**. Two steps are manageable, but with three or four the brackets pile up. In Session 2 you'll learn the **pipe** `%>%`, which writes the same steps in order, from left to right.
:::

::: callout-note
## Conditions you can use in `filter()`

`==` equal · `!=` not equal · `>` `<` `>=` `<=` · `%in% c(...)` one of several values · `is.na()` missing · `&` and · `|` or

Use `==` (two equals signs) to compare. One `=` is for naming arguments.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 6 (3 min): zooming in

Sort `measles_raw` by `` `Temp (C)` ``, largest first, and show only the top 10 rows. What is the highest temperature? What do you think happened?

Pattern: `head(arrange(DATA, desc(COLUMN)), 10)`

✅ **Check:** the top value is 104.7

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
head(arrange(measles_raw, desc(`Temp (C)`)), 10)
```

104.7 is about 40 °C written in **Fahrenheit**. A few temperatures were entered in °F instead of °C.
:::
:::

## Missing values and duplicates

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.6** — Missing values with `colSums(is.na())`, rows with no Case ID, and duplicates with `sum(duplicated())` and `get_dupes()`.
:::

```{r}
# Missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(linelist_raw))

# How many rows have no Case ID? Count the rows that filter() keeps
nrow(filter(linelist_raw, is.na(`Case ID`)))

# How many rows are exact copies of an earlier row?
sum(duplicated(linelist_raw))
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Look at the duplicated rows (shows every copy, plus a dupe_count column)
get_dupes(linelist_raw)
```

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 7 (3 min): missing values and duplicates

In `measles_raw`:

a)  How many rows have a missing `` `Patient ID` ``?
b)  How many rows are exact duplicates?
c)  Which column has the most missing values? Is that a mistake, or does it make sense?

✅ **Check:** a) 37 b) 15

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
nrow(filter(measles_raw, is.na(`Patient ID`)))
sum(duplicated(measles_raw))
colSums(is.na(measles_raw))
```

c)  `Days in Hospital` has the most (766). That makes sense: patients who were never hospitalized have no hospital days. **Missing is not always an error!**
:::
:::

# Part 6: The problem list

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 6.1** — The problem list for `linelist_raw`, filled in together.
:::

Here is everything we found in `linelist_raw`. This list is the to-do list for Session 2.

| \# | Problem | How we found it |
|----|---------|-----------------|
| 1 | Column names have spaces, dots, and capitals | `names()` |
| 2 | Date columns are different types (`date.onset` is text) | `glimpse()` |
| 3 | `age` is stored as text, and 37 ages are in **months** not years | `glimpse()`, `count()` |
| 4 | Hospital names are misspelled ("Hopital") or inconsistent ("Regional MC"), and many are missing | `count()` |
| 5 | Gender and outcome have missing values | `count()`, `skim()` |
| 6 | Impossible weights (negative, 0) and heights (4 cm, 295 cm) | `skim()`, `arrange()` |
| 7 | 130 rows have no Case ID | `is.na()` |
| 8 | 25 rows are duplicates | `duplicated()` |

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 8 (10 min): the measles problem list

Write a numbered problem list for `measles_raw` in your student script, using everything you found in the TRY ITs. Save it — you will fix these problems in Session 2!

✅ **Check:** you should find at least 8 problems

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

1.  Column names have spaces, capitals, and symbols (`?` and parentheses)
2.  `Age (years)` is stored as text because of "unknown" (27 rows) and "999" (4 rows)
3.  District is misspelled ("Nroth", "Cetnral"), has lower-case versions, and some say "... District"
4.  SEX is written 6 different ways (Male / male / M, Female / female / F)
5.  `Vaccinated?` is written 8 different ways (Yes / yes / Y, No / no / N / NO, Unknown)
6.  Outcome has inconsistent capitalization and 68 missing values
7.  Some temperatures were entered in Fahrenheit (values around 97–105)
8.  37 rows have no Patient ID
9.  15 rows are duplicates
10. `Report Date`, District, and SEX have some missing values
:::
:::

::: callout-tip
## ⭐ Bonus: your own data

Brought your own dataset? Put the file in the `raw_data/` folder, then: `import()` it; look at it with `dim()`, `glimpse()`, and `skim()`; `count()` its text columns to look for misspellings; check for missing values and duplicates; and write its problem list.
:::

# Key points

-   `<-` saves a value in an object; `c()` makes a vector; functions take arguments.
-   **Install** a package once with `install.packages()`; **load** it every session with `library()`.
-   A **project folder** plus `here()` makes file paths work on any computer.
-   `import(here("folder", "file"))` reads almost any file type.
-   **Look before you clean:** `glimpse()`, `skim()`, `count()`, `filter()`, `arrange()`, `is.na()`, and `duplicated()` find the problems.
-   To do two steps, put one function inside another: `head(arrange(data, column), 10)`. Wrap long output in `head()`.

**Next: Session 2 — Cleaning.** We start with the **pipe** `%>%`, then fix the problem list with `clean_names()`, `mutate()`, `if_else()`, and `case_when()`.
